Then I repeated to myself the beautiful passage about Dante entering Paradise on earth. I imagined walking beside those lovely banks and seeing a shining chariot descend, bringing back the father I had lost so long ago. How sweet that would be. While waiting for that moment, I imagined gathering the lovely flowers around me, weaving them into a wreath, and crowning myself with joy. I would sing my father’s favourite song, ‘sul margine d’un rio.’ My voice would travel through the windless air and tell him that his daughter had come, wherever he sat among the leafy shelters, waiting for us to meet again. The signs of misery would have faded from my face by then, and I could look into his eyes without fear. Those eyes had always shone with the soft light of innocent love. Thinking of their deep, magical expression made me cry, but I wept gently, so my sobs would not break the spell of the scene.

I was so lost in this dream that I kept walking without noticing where I went. At last I bent down to pick a flower for my wreath, though I was on a bleak plain where no flowers grew. Only then did I come out of my daydream and realise I did not know where I was.

The sun was down, and the pink colour it had given the clouds while setting had almost disappeared. A wind blew across the plain. I looked around for something I recognised, but nothing showed me where I was. I had lost my way, and all my efforts to find the path failed. I kept wandering as the growing darkness made any possible landmarks harder to see. Finally, the deepest black night hid everything. I was tired. My servant was staying that night in the nearby village, so nobody would worry about my absence. This wild place also kept me safe from anyone who might intrude. I decided to spend the night there. In fact, I was too weary to go any farther. The air was chilly, but physical discomfort did not concern me. I believed my two years of solitude had made me used to the weather: throughout that time, the changing seasons had never stopped my endless walks.

I lay on the grass, surrounded by darkness that not even the smallest beam of light could enter. Nothing made a sound. The deep night had sent the insects to sleep; they were the only creatures living in this lonely place, with no trees or bushes to shelter anything else. A wonderful silence filled the air. It quieted my senses but brought my soul to life. My thoughts raced from image to image, and my mind seemed able to hold all eternity.

But it is most remarkable that she always hears Jane more readily than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she will find her grandmama no deafer than she was two years ago, which is a great deal to say at my mother’s age—and it really has been two full years since her last visit, you know. We have never before gone so long without seeing her; and, as I said to Mrs. Cole, we shall scarcely know how to make enough fuss over her now.”

“Do you expect Miss Fairfax to visit soon?”

“Oh, yes, next week.”

“Indeed! That must give you very great pleasure.”

“Thank you; how kind you are. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone makes the same obliging remarks. I am certain she will be just as glad to see her Highbury friends as they will be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot specify which, for Colonel Campbell needs the carriage himself on one of those days. How very good of them to convey her the entire way! But they always do, of course. Oh yes, next Friday or Saturday. That is the subject of her letter. It accounts for her writing outside her rule, as we say; ordinarily we would have had no word from her until Tuesday or Wednesday next.”

“Yes, that was what I supposed. I feared there was little prospect of hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today.”

“How obliging! No, we would not have heard, except for this particular circumstance—her coming here so soon. My mother is quite delighted! For she will stay with us at least three months. Three months, she states it quite positively, as I shall have the pleasure of reading to you. You see, the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her father and mother to come and visit her immediately. They had meant to wait until summer, but she is so eager to see them again—for before her marriage last October, she had never spent so much as a week away from them. It must feel very odd to be in separate kingdoms, I was about to say, but separate countries, at any rate. So she sent a most pressing letter to her mother—or perhaps her father; I declare I cannot remember which, but Jane’s letter will tell us presently—writing in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, to urge them to come over directly. They would meet them in Dublin and bring them back to their country estate, Baly-craig, which I fancy is a beautiful place.

At the steps where we had taken him aboard, and throughout the time since, I had kept a watchful eye for any indication that we were suspected. There had been none. We had certainly not been accompanied or pursued by another boat, nor were we being followed then. Had a boat kept attending us, I would have turned toward the shore and forced it either to continue onward or reveal its intention. But we maintained our course without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and appeared, as I have said, entirely at home in the scene. Remarkably—though perhaps his miserable past explained it—he was less anxious than any of us. This was not indifference: he told me he hoped to live to see his gentleman become one of the finest gentlemen in a foreign land. Nor, as I understood him, was he inclined toward passivity or resignation. He simply had no thought of going halfway to meet a danger. Once it reached him, he faced it, but it had to arrive before he would trouble himself about it.

“If you knowed, dear boy,” he told me, “what sitting here with my dear boy and having a smoke means, after spending day after day shut between four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it means.”

“I believe I understand the pleasures of freedom,” I replied.

“Ah,” he said, gravely shaking his head, “but you don’t understand ’em like me. You’d have to have been locked up, dear boy, to know ’em as I do—but I ain’t going to grow downhearted.”

It struck me as contradictory that any overriding purpose should have led him to risk his freedom, and indeed his life. Yet I considered that freedom without peril might be so far removed from his lifelong experience that it meant something different to him than to another man. I was not much mistaken, for after smoking a while he said:

“You see, dear boy, while I was over there, on the far side of the world, my eyes was always turned this way. It felt flat being there, though I was getting rich. Everyone knowed Magwitch; Magwitch could come and go, and nobody troubled their heads over him. They ain’t so easy about me here, dear boy—leastways, they wouldn’t be if they knowed where I was.”

“If things go well,” I said, “in a few hours you will be entirely free and safe once more.”

“Well,” he replied, taking a deep breath, “I hope I shall.”

“And do you believe it?”
